caption: Glass Squid We call Earth the Blue Planet for a reason — it's a lot of water! The water column, which includes all of the water in the ocean between the surface and the seafloor, makes up 95-99% of the total livable volume of the planet, yet remains one of the most poorly explored environments on Earth. But the glimpses of life in the water column we do get tend to be pretty amazing.

caption: Sea Spider Did you know that sea spiders are not actually spiders? Doesn't really make them any less creepy, but still... Get the facts on sea spiders .

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-Sea Exploration
caption: Chimaera This cute chimaera stopped to say hello to remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer during a dive off the coast of Florida, giving us a good view of the lateral lines running across its head that allow it to detect pressure waves (like our ears). The dotted-looking lines near the fish’s mouth are ampullae of Lorenzini that can detect perturbations in electrical fields generated by living organisms. Hey little, buddy!

credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 Cook Islands ROV Exploration
caption: and Education Resources video Cusk Eel This faceless cusk eel was seen during Dive 06 of the 2026 Cook Islands ROV Exploration cruise. This fish gets its common name from the fact that it appears to hardly have a face. Its mouth is on the underside of its head, but it lacks visible eyes. It navigates through the water using two pairs of large nostrils on the front of its head. The scientific name for these fish, Typhlonus nasus, translates from Greek and Latin to mean a large-nosed, blind hake.
